item.title: Global shares drop on AI worries, echoing Wall Street's decline despite the strong Anthropic debut
item.description: Global shares dropped in Friday trading as a wide selloff hits issues related to artificial intelligence and computer chips.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks on Friday pulled the S&P 500 down 3.7 per cent, dragging the index to its worst weekly loss in more than 18 months, and knocking the Nasdaq composite into the red for the year. The benchmark index is now in what professional investors call a “correction,” having fallen more than 10 per cent from its Oct. 6 all-time high. The last time the S&P 500 had a correction was March 2025, as the Trump administration’s trade war rattled the market. Its weekly loss, marking its worst such decline since April 2025, as the trade war escalated, capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest such string of losses since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The Nasdaq composite, which is more greatly influenced by tech stocks, slumped 5.3 per cent, pulling it into negative territory for the year. Its weekly loss was also just shy of its worst week since March 2020, when the pandemic ground the global economy to a halt. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, with less exposure to technology stocks, fell 1.9 per cent. Chip stocks like Nvidia, Micron Technology, Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices bore the brunt of the selling, but other companies connected to the AI buildout tanked as well, including the optical products company Corning and the energy provider Bloom Energy. The AI lab Anthropic, coming off a successful IPO Thursday, tumbled 9.1 per cent. The sell-off in technology stocks spread around the globe: Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s Kospi each fell more than 5 per cent overnight. European indexes fell sharply as well. AI stocks have hefty market values and have a much bigger impact on the market’s direction. They were responsible for Wall Street’s big gains this year and are now behind the big slide for the market. The AI trade has been losing steam partly over worries that AI stocks’ big market values and heavy spending are unjustified. Fears of a bubble within the sector have also been exacerbated by the results of the recent midterm elections, with candidates advocating for a slowdown in data centre construction winning at both the federal and state level. “The whole notion that AI can continue to spend unlimited amounts of money and support the stock market, I think the notion of that is ending as we speak, that’s what’s being priced right now,” said Michael Antonelli, market strategist at Baird. “But I don’t think that means that the overall bull market that started in October 2022 is over.” Much of the AI rout was centreed among chip stocks, which have been big beneficiaries of the build out of AI data centres. Advanced Micro Devices sank 13.3 per cent, Micron Technology slid 13.9 per cent and Broadcom fell 12.1 per cent. The PHLX Semiconductor Index sank 10.7 per cent. Corning slid 10.9 per cent and Bloom Energy gave up 15.3 per cent. Nvidia, considered by many to be the poster child for the AI boom, fell for the ninth day in the last 10, closing 13.8 per cent lower. The chip company’s stock was caught up in the market’s anxiety about the strength of the AI build out, and more recently has been pressured by worries about its future following the sudden downfall of Jensen Huang, its former CEO and co-founder. Since the Huang scandal erupted earlier this month, the stock has dropped more than 25 per cent. The big market debut for Anthropic, maker of the Claude AI tool, fizzled Friday with the rest of the tech sector. The stock fell 9.1 per cent to US$88.30, but remains above its IPO price of US$83 per share. It was the biggest public stock offering ever, at one point surpassing US$2 trillion in value. Anthropic’s share price drop on Friday amounts to a roughly 23 per cent decline from its brief peak of US$115.10 a share set the day prior. That’s an even bigger drop than the dive seen for Facebook (now Meta) in the early days after its May 2012 IPO. Market debuts for tech companies are often followed by a volatile period. SpaceX, which previously held the title for biggest IPO, rose nearly 50 per cent in its first three days, but fell below its IPO price a month later. Outside of tech, though, most stocks were gaining ground. Cheerios maker General Mills rose 3.7 per cent and homebuilder Lennar gained 1 per cent. All told, the S&P 500 fell 265.44 points to 6,910.39. The Dow dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33, and the Nasdaq lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73. While the stock market’s mood has soured, the sentiment among American consumers appears to have brightened, a reversal of the dynamic seen earlier this year. The University of Michigan’s latest index of consumer sentiment rose sharply compared to last month, coming in slightly ahead of economists’ expectations. Consumers noted some relief from easing gas prices and improved expectations for business conditions following the midterm elections. Still, sentiment remains below where it was in February, before the start of the U.S. war with Iran. Treasury yields fell in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.93 per cent from 5.04 per cent late Thursday. Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 0.6 per cent to settle at US$92.57 per barrel, amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz as the U.S. war with Iran continues. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels had fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom days after it launched a major air campaign across Houthi-controlled parts of Yemen. Iraq apparently reached a compromise with a powerful Iran-backed militia it accused of smuggling oil. ___ Damian J. Troise and Alex Veiga, The Associated Press AP Business Writers Yuri Kageyama and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report.

item.title: Hot Picks: Three U.S. aerospace and defence stocks to watch
item.description: RBC Capital Markets analyst Ken Herbert discusses three U.S. aerospace and defence stocks: GE Aerospace, VSE Corp. and Mercury Systems.
item.dc:creator: BNN Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: The U.S. aerospace and defence sector spans businesses that sell aircraft parts, service jet engines and supply military electronics. Those businesses rely on different sources of demand. BNN Bloomberg spoke with Ken Herbert, analyst at RBC Capital Markets, about what he looks for in each part of the sector. Key Takeaways Read the full transcript below: LINDSAY: It’s time now for Hot Picks. Today we are focusing on the aerospace sector, with demand for aircraft maintenance continuing to grow and defence companies new opportunities. Should investors be looking? Let’s get more now from Ken Herbert, analyst at RBC Capital Markets. It’s great to have you join us this morning. Thank you. KEN: Thanks for having me. Great to be here. LINDSAY: Do you think, before we get into actual Hot Picks, like, do you think the aerospace sector is entering a new growth phase? KEN: I wouldn’t say it’s a new growth phase, but I would certainly say this is one of the longest cycles I can certainly remember in my 30 years of covering the sector. So, which means, in my view, we still have significant runway in this sector. So, not necessarily a new phase, but continues to be very attractive in terms of long-term fundamentals. LINDSAY: Okay, let’s get into it then. GE Aerospace is your first pick today. Tell us why you like this company right now. KEN: We like GE Aerospace because, one, we feel like the services market not as negative or not as, not as soft as people fear. You think about GE, 40 per cent of its services revenue — and services does account for three-quarters of its commercial business — 40 per cent of that business is wide-body aircraft. We think the wide-body aircraft are going to see a real step up in services in the next one to two years, helping to offset any concern or incremental risk on the narrow-body portfolio. On the narrow-body portfolio, we think the LEAP engine, in terms of its long-term value, continues to be underappreciated by investors. The fleet of that engine is expected to double over the next five years, which will provide a very significant tailwind on the services side. And we would just finally mention that, as you look at GE, it’s a business that perhaps, arguably, in our view, one of the best in terms of execution within the aerospace and defence sector, consistently outperforming expectations, and we think you’ve got some very nice reason to believe that execution outperformance will continue through 2027 into 2028. LINDSAY: A lot of that growth so far has been driven by demand for engine servicing and maintenance. What can investors watch for, like, as you say, through 2027 and 2028? What can investors watch for to kind of ensure that that momentum will continue? KEN: Well, it all starts and stops with passenger travel, right? I mean, travel globally has remained extremely resilient over the last three to four years. Fair to assume we’ve seen, or fair to say, we’ve seen some stepbacks in travel this year, just considering some of the geopolitical uncertainty. But we haven’t seen nearly the kind of demand destruction that we feared we would have seen as crude prices surged through the summer and into the early fall of this year. But we’re very focused on travel and demand. The airlines have remained financially very sound and very healthy through this crisis this year. So as that continues to hold up and travel remains robust, I think that underpins a lot of the bullish thesis, in our view, around the services side for GE. LINDSAY: Okay, next up is VSE Corporation. You believe that VSE can grow faster than its peers. Tell us more about that. KEN: Yeah, so the company, the summer of this year, closed a large acquisition, basically doubling the size of the business organically. It’s got a very healthy mix between business jets and commercial transport aircraft, so it skews a little bit more towards business jets. We feel like it’s got significant pricing power across its portfolio, but you’re seeing a very inorganic contribution with better than pure organic growth as it continues to take share in both its distribution and its component repair businesses. So VSEC is basically 100 per cent commercial aerospace aftermarket. LINDSAY: It is looking at ways to improve profitability. Where do you see the biggest opportunity for the company to continue to grow its margins? KEN: It’s a great question. We think this will be a real catalyst for the stock as we start to think about an investor day the company is hosting in a couple of weeks in New York. I’d point to really two or three areas. The first is just mix, obviously, with the recent acquisition and with synergy opportunities across that acquisition and other recent acquisitions that present significant opportunities. Second, we’re seeing a mix shift in the business as it gets more involved in areas where it owns IP and has more margin potential there. And third, I would just say execution, especially on its distribution side, where it’s management team that, in our view, has proven extremely good and adept at finding ways to create value for its OEM partners, which is helping to translate to margin opportunity for the business. LINDSAY: Okay, let’s get to your last pick, then. It is Mercury Systems. Tell us why you like Mercury Systems. KEN: So Mercury Systems, our only company on this list with significant defence exposure. It’s basically a merchant supplier of electronics and defence computing systems, predominantly to the United States government and international allies. Mercury has a very significant idiosyncratic story around margin expansion and free cash flow expansion. The company improved gross margins and operating margins by almost 700 basis points in its most recent quarter. It’s coming out, coming out of a very significant investment phase and entering a very significant harvest phase, which should continue to drive margin expansion through better mix, as well as obviously a significant free cash flow, basically doubling of free cash flow in the next two years off of ’26 levels. It is obviously facing some overhang from sentiment on defence spending, but we view the company as well positioned to continue to drive double-digit growth as a merchant supplier across defence electronics. LINDSAY: Why is that? Like, how sustainable do you really think it, think it is long term for a company like Mercury? KEN: Two things I would say. One, we are seeing, in our view, in a worst-case scenario, low to, low to mid-single-digit growth in overall defence spending globally, with the United States the biggest market, but stronger growth in other regions, but even still growth in the United States. But more importantly, the electronic content, as weapons systems and the military incorporate more AI, incorporate upgrades, incorporate more sophistication, whether they be around drones, missiles, missile defence. Mercury, as the supplier of the hardware to make that happen, in our view, means you see almost two times growth for Mercury in the electronic side is what you’ll see in just broader budget growth. And again, as a merchant supplier, they’re not dependent on any one particular platform, system or particular market. LINDSAY: Okay, we’ll leave it there because we’re just about out of time. Ken Herbert, analyst at RBC Capital Markets. Great to have you join us. Thank you. --- This BNN Bloomberg summary and transcript of the Nov. 20, 2026 interview with Ken Herbert are published with the assistance of AI. item.title: Canada’s economy ‘much weaker’ than many expected, says expert after sluggish retail sales report
item.description: Canada’s economic woes were on full display Friday, according to one financial expert who says the country’s latest retail sales figures were disappointing, and they’re expected to get worse.
item.dc:creator: Jordan Fleguel
item.content:encoded: Canada’s economic woes were on full display Friday, according to one financial expert who says the country’s latest retail sales figures were disappointing, and they’re expected to get worse. “The Canadian economy is sort of, not on life support, but it has gotten much weaker than I think people were expecting,” Paul Harris, portfolio manager at Harris Douglas Asset Management, told BNN Bloomberg on Friday. “I think it’s a reflection of many of the issues that we’re facing from a trade basis, but also kind of a global slump that’s going through the world right now.” Harris’ comments came after Statistics Canada (StatCan) released retail sales data for September, which showed a modest 0.8 per cent increase, boosted mainly by higher prices at gas stations and other fuel vendors. Core retail sales, which exclude those segments of the economy as well as motor vehicle and parts dealers, rose just 0.1 per cent in September. “A lot of it was gasoline, so from a regional basis there were some differences, but I think overall, it was not a good number, and October doesn’t look like it’s going to be a good number,” Harris said. StatCan’s preliminary flash estimate for retail sales last month shows them dropping 1.5 per cent. “I think that you’re seeing this kind of slowdown in the Canadian economy and all the issues with tariffs and stuff like that catching up to us in the last little while,” argued Harris. ‘Better than expected’ Sal Guatieri, director and senior economist at BMO Capital Markets, says retail sales growth has slowed in the second half of 2026 after a solid start to the year, but he also noted that September’s final retail sales figure came in slightly higher than StatCan’s initial estimate of 0.7 per cent. “It was a little better than expected, and a little better than StatCan initially estimated for September,” he told BNN Bloomberg on Friday. “(It was) nice to see some upward revision to the August figure as well, with a more than one per cent gain there, but there were a couple of disappointments though.” Firstly, Guatieri said, much of September’s retail sales increase was price related, driven by higher costs for gasoline and fuel but also for other consumer goods, he noted. “So, the volume increase is probably not all that great,” Guatieri said, “and the more worrisome thing is the flash estimate for October… that sets a pretty weak stage and setup for fourth quarter spending.” Still, Canadian consumer spending has “been holding pretty tough” so far this year, he argued, growing nearly two per cent in real terms in 2026 through the second quarter. “It does seem like consumers at least are hanging in there,” said Guatieri. Though still elevated, gasoline prices have started to fall in Canada due to changing global supply and demand dynamics. Lower fuel prices will improve Canadians’ purchasing power heading into the important holiday retail season, but many shoppers remain wary of other affordability issues such as inflation and rising interest rates.
